(a) the SFR is correlated with LX, at all red and LX spanned in our sample, (b) there is an enhancement of sSFR with LX, (c) the AGN enhances or suppresses the star-formation, depending on whether the galaxy is above or below the main sequence.
the X-ray AGN enhances the SFR of their hosts, when the host is below the main sequence, and suppresses the SFR of its host, when the host resides above the main sequence.
the AGN-SFR connection is a strong function of the location of the host galaxy on the main sequence and that this effect is present at all redz, i.e., from the local universe to redz ~3.

AGN enhance star-formation in galaxies below the MS, and quench the star-formation in the galaxies above the main sequence, at all redshifts and X-ray luminosities.
the AGN activity is not correlated with the SFR of their host galaxies but with the location of the host galaxy on the main sequence.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AGN enhance the star-formation in low-mass, low redshift galaxies, while they quench star-formation in massive, high redshift galaxies.

X-ray AGN are more likely to enhance the star-formation rate of the host galaxy at lower redz, when the galaxy is below the main sequence, while at high redz, the AGN are more efficient to quench star-formation of galaxies above the main sequence.

the LX of AGN correlates with the SFR of their hosts, but the effect of AGNs on the SFRs of their hosts, depends on redz, M* and the location of the host galaxy relative to the star-formation main sequence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AGN enhance the star-formation rate (SFR) of the host galaxy only when the host galaxy is below the star-forming main sequence.
the LX of the AGN correlates with the SFR of its host galaxy at all redz, LX and M* and that this effect is more prominent when the host galaxy lies below the star formation main sequence.
the LX is not a good indicator of the SFR, since the SFR is affected by the redz and M* of the galaxy.
